rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited verse does not say that the man had been a saint and then lost sainthood.
rows.anchor: فليس في الآية أنه كان وليا ثم انسلخت عنه الولاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports that wonders resembling saintly miracles appeared through him are solitary reports and do not establish knowledge.
rows.anchor: وما نقل أنه ظهر على يديه ما يجري مجرى الكرامات هو أخبار آحاد لا توجب العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One definition distinguishes a saintly wonder, whose condition is concealment, from a prophetic miracle, whose condition is public display.
rows.anchor: الكرامة من شرطها الاستتار، والمعجزة من شرطها الإظهار

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another definition says a karama appears without a claim, while a prophetic miracle follows a prophet's claim and challenge to produce proof.
rows.anchor: الكرامة ما تظهر من غير دعوى، والمعجزة ما تظهر عند دعوى الأنبياء

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari's report recounts the ambush of ten scouts led by Asim ibn Thabit; seven were killed and three surrendered under a treaty.
rows.anchor: من حديث أبي هريرة قال: بعث رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عشرة رهط سرية عينا

rows.speaker: عاصم بن ثابت
rows.claim: Asim refused the attackers' protection because he would not accept a nonbeliever's guarantee, and prayed that the Prophet be told what happened.
rows.anchor: أما فوالله لا أنزل اليوم في ذمة الكافر، اللهم أخبر عنا نبيك

rows.speaker: بنت الحارث
rows.claim: Khubayb ate fresh grapes while shackled in Mecca, where no fruit was then available; his captor regarded them as provision from God.
rows.anchor: إنه لرزق رزقه الله تعالى خبيبا

rows.speaker: خبيب الأنصاري
rows.claim: Before execution, Khubayb prayed two units and said he would have lengthened them if people would not mistake it for fear of death; he established this practice for Muslims executed as captives.
rows.anchor: فركع ركعتين ثم قال: لولا أن تظنوا أن ما بي جزع من الموت لزدت

rows.speaker: خبيب الأنصاري
rows.claim: Khubayb prayed that God count and kill his persecutors separately and leave none alive.
rows.anchor: اللهم أحصهم عددا، واقتلهم بددا، ولا تبق منهم أحدا

rows.speaker: خبيب الأنصاري
rows.claim: His execution poem says he does not care which side receives his Muslim body, since his death is for God and God may bless his dismembered remains.
rows.anchor: ولست أبالي حين أقتل مسلما على أي شق كان لله مصرعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God answered Asim's prayer by informing the Prophet and companions about the expedition and its losses.
rows.anchor: فاستجاب الله تعالى لعاصم يوم أصيب فأخبر النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام وأصحابه خبرهم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: When Quraysh sought Asim's body for identification, wasps protected it and prevented them from cutting away any flesh.
rows.anchor: فبعث الله على عاصم مثل الظلة من الدبر فحمته من رسلهم

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Hudhayl sought Asim's head for a woman who had vowed to drink wine from his skull; wasps kept them from it, then a flood carried the body away.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن إسحاق في هذه القصة: وقد كانت هذيل حين قتل عاصم بن ثابت أرادوا رأسه

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq adds that Asim vowed never to touch a polytheist or be touched by one, and God protected him after death as in life.
rows.anchor: وقد كان عاصم أعطى الله تعالى عهدا ألا يمس مشركا ولا يمسه مشرك أبدا

rows.speaker: عمرو بن أمية الضمري
rows.claim: Amr ibn Umayya says he released Khubayb's body from its stake; after he stepped away, it seemed to sink into the earth, and al-Bayhaqi transmits a version saying no trace remained.
rows.anchor: وعن عمرو بن أمية الضمري: وكان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بعثه عينا وحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A saint may own land and wealth to preserve his dignity and support his family; the Companions' property despite their sanctity is precedent.
rows.anchor: ولا ينكر أن يكون للولي مال وضيعة يصون بها وجهه وعياله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report describes a cloud ordered to water a named man's garden; he divided its yield among charity, his household, and reinvestment.
rows.anchor: سمع صوتا في سحابة اسق حديقة فلان فتنحى ذلك السحاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A variant assigns one third of the garden's yield to the poor, petitioners, and wayfarers.
rows.anchor: وأجعل ثلثه في المساكين والسائلين وابن السبيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning against farms targets accumulation and luxury; earning a livelihood to protect one's faith and dependents is excellent.
rows.anchor: وأما من اتخذها معاشا يصون بها دينه وعياله فاتخاذها بهذه النية من أفضل الأعمال

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet's saying that sound wealth is good for a righteous man supports property used virtuously.
rows.anchor: نعم المال الصالح للرجل الصالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wage Moses mentioned at the wall supports the permissibility of hiring, a practice of prophets and saints.
rows.anchor: فيه دليل على صحة جواز الإجارة، وهي سنة الأنبياء والأولياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers say lattaḫaḏta; Abu Amr, Ibn Masud, Hasan, and Qatada read lattaḫiḏta, dialect forms of the same verb; readers differ on assimilation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «لاتخذت» وأبو عمرو «لتخذت» وهي قراءة ابن مسعود والحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kab's hadith wording is: if you wished, you would have been given a wage.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أبي بن كعب: لو شئت لأوتيت أجرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' wage suggestion was an offer, not an objection; Khidr declared the separation required by Moses' own condition.
rows.anchor: وهذه صدرت من موسى سؤالا على جهة العرض لا الاعتراض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “between me and you” instead of “between us” adds emphasis, as Sibawayh's example illustrates.
rows.anchor: وتكريره «بيني وبينك» وعدوله عن بيننا لمعنى التأكيد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Moses' remarks on the ship and boy were for God, while his wall comment sought something worldly and caused the parting.
rows.anchor: وكان قول موسى في السفينة والغلام لله، وكان قوله في الجدار لنفسه

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says the wall stood one hundred cubits high.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب بن منبه: كان ذلك الجدار جدارا طوله في السماء مائة ذراع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ta'wil means eventual outcome; Khidr promised to explain why he acted as he did.
rows.anchor: تأويل الشيء مآله أي قال له: إني أخبرك لم فعلت ما فعلت

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation treats the episodes as evidence against Moses, not marvels, comparing each objection with his earlier experience or action.
rows.anchor: إنها حجة على موسى، لا عجبا له

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The ship objection is answered by recalling Moses as an infant placed in a chest and cast into the river.
rows.anchor: أين كان تدبيرك هذا وأنت في التابوت مطروحا في اليم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The objection to killing the boy is answered by recalling Moses' blow that killed the Egyptian.
rows.anchor: أين إنكارك هذا من وكزك القبطي وقضائك عليه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The complaint over the wall is answered by recalling that Moses raised a well-stone for Shuayb's daughters without payment.
rows.anchor: أين هذا من رفعك حجر البئر لبنات شعيب دون أجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi cites the verse as evidence for the view that a miskin is better off than a faqir.
rows.anchor: استدل بهذا من قال: إن المسكين أحسن حالا من الفقير

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Others say merchants were called needy because travel, scarcity, and vulnerability at sea made them pitiable; even a rich person in distress may be called miskin.
rows.anchor: كانوا تجارا ولكن من حيث هم مسافرون عن قلة في لجة بحر

rows.speaker: كعب وغيره
rows.claim: Ka'b and others say ten needy brothers inherited the boat: five were disabled and five worked at sea.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب وغيره: كانت لعشرة إخوة من المساكين ورثوها من أبيهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another report says seven brothers each had a different disability.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانوا سبعة لكل واحد منهم زمانة ليست بالاخر

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash lists the workers' and nonworkers' disabilities, including leprosy, one-eyedness, lameness, fever, blindness, deafness, muteness, paralysis, and madness.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكر النقاش أسماءهم فأما العمال منهم فأحدهم كان مجذوما

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: Al-Tha'labi says their sea route ran between Persia and Rome.
rows.anchor: وكان البحر الذي يعملون فيه ما بين فارس والروم ذكره الثعلبي

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: A group reads the word with doubled sīn and takes it to mean sailors, from the word for one who holds a vessel or its crew.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة: «لمساكين» بتشديد السين، واختلف في ذلك فقيل: هم ملاحو السفينة

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group derives the doubled form from misk, meaning hides, and interprets it as tanners of skins.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: أراد بالمساكين دبغة المسوك وهي الجلود واحدها مسك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stronger reading is the ordinary light-sīn plural miskīn, referring to vulnerable poor people deserving sympathy.
rows.anchor: والأظهر قراءة «مساكين» بالتخفيف جمع مسكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿībaha means to make the ship defective; ʿāba means something becomes defective.
rows.anchor: أي أجعلها ذات عيب، يقال: عبت الشيء فعاب إذا صار ذا عيب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr read “sound”; Ibn Abbas and Uthman also read “fit.”
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عباس وابن جبير «صحيحة» وقرأ أيضا ابن عباس وعثمان بن عفان «صالحة»

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some commentators take wara'ahum in its usual sense, “behind them,” and say the king would catch them on their return.
rows.anchor: فقال بعض المفسرين: إنه كان خلفه وكان رجوعهم عليه

rows.speaker: الأكثر
rows.claim: Most commentators understand wara'ahum as “in front of them,” supported by variant readings.
rows.anchor: والأكثر على أن معنى «وراء» هنا أمام

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد وأبو علي قطرب
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd and Abu Ali Qutrub treat wara as an antonym meaning “in front”; Ibn Arafa rejects this as inadequate because front and behind are opposites.
rows.anchor: فزعم أبو عبيد وأبو علي قطرب أن هذا من الأضداد

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri allows wara for what lies ahead in time but not as a spatial synonym of amam.
rows.anchor: وأشار إلى هذا القول أيضا القشيري وقال: إنما يقال هذا في الأوقات

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra reports that some others allowed this usage beyond temporal contexts.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: وجوزه غيره

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: The crew did not know the king's plan; God informed Khidr, enabling him to damage the vessel in advance.
rows.anchor: والقوم ما كانوا عالمين بخبر الملك، فأخبر الله تعالى الخضر حتى عيب السفينة

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi gives three analyses: wara as a general antonym for ahead, its use ahead only for time, or its use ahead for faceless physical objects such as two stones; the last is attributed to Ali ibn Isa.
rows.anchor: اختلف أهل العربية في استعمال وراء موضع أمام على ثلاثة أقوال

rows.speaker: الماوردي
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi cites the verse about Hell behind people and a poem using wara for what lies before the speaker.
rows.anchor: قال الله تعالى: من ورآئهم جهنم

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A cited poem uses wara'iya to mean “before me,” illustrating the antonym usage.
rows.anchor: وقومي تميم والفلاة ورائيا يعني أمامي

rows.speaker: ابن عرفة
rows.claim: Ibn Arafa illustrates the temporal sense with a promise for Ramadan followed by saying Sha'ban lies wara the addressee, although it is earlier in calendar order.
rows.anchor: كقولك للرجل إذا وعد وعدا في رجب لرمضان ثم قال: ومن ورائك شعبان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word can be explained according to time and place, resolving its apparent difficulty.
rows.anchor: وإنما يصلح هذا في الأماكن والأوقات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The king's name is variously given as Hadad ibn Baddad or al-Julanda, according to al-Suhayli.
rows.anchor: واختلف في اسم هذا الملك فقيل: هدد بن بدد. وقيل: الجلندي وقاله السهيلي

rows.speaker: البخاري
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari names the king Hadad ibn Baddad and the slain boy Jaysur, with manuscript variants Haysur and Haysun.
rows.anchor: وذكر البخاري اسم الملك الآخذ لكل سفينة غصبا فقال: هو هدد بن بدد والغلام المقتول اسمه جيسور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode permits using public benefit as a legal consideration and repairing a whole asset by sacrificing part of it.
rows.anchor: فقه العمل بالمصالح إذا تحقق وجهها، وجواز إصلاح كل المال بإفساد بعضه

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report in Sahih Muslim says the king passed over the boat after seeing its defect and its owners repaired it with a plank.
rows.anchor: فإذا جاء الذي يسخرها وجدها منخرقة فتجاوزها، فأصلحوها بخشبة الحديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story encourages patience in hardship because disliked events may contain benefits, as in the cited verse.
rows.anchor: وتحصل من هذا الحض على الصبر في الشدائد، فكم في ضمن ذلك المكروه من الفوائد

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A sound hadith says the boy was created a disbeliever, supporting the apparent inference he was not an adult; it could instead describe him while grown.
rows.anchor: أنه طبع يوم طبع كافرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators take “we feared” as Khidr's own speech, and the context supports this; God had permitted his judgment to kill in this circumstance.
rows.anchor: وهو الذي يشهد له سياق الكلام، وهو قول كثير من المفسرين

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas take “we feared” as God's speech conveyed by Khidr, meaning “we knew.”
rows.anchor: قال الطبري: معناه فعلمنا وكذا قال ابن عباس أي فعلمنا

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy's reading replaces “we feared” with “your Lord knew.”
rows.anchor: وحكي أن أبيا قرأ «فعلم ربك»

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes khashiya to mean aversion or dislike rather than fear.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الخشية بمعنى الكراهة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya calls the interpretation a metaphor from the perspective of human listeners who would fear the boy's effect on his parents; Ibn Masud's reading supports this.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: والأظهر عندي في توجيه هذا التأويل وإن كان اللفظ يدافعه أنها استعارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expressions of hope and fear attributed to God reflect the hearers' perspective, not divine uncertainty.
rows.anchor: إنما هو بحسبكم أيها المخاطبون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yurhiq means to burden or compel them; parental love would make them follow the boy and stray into his religion.
rows.anchor: «يرهقهما» يجشمهما ويكلفهما والمعنى أن يلقيهما حبه في اتباعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers have yubaddilahuma with an open bāʾ and doubled dāl; Asim reads yubdilahuma with a quiescent bāʾ and light dāl, meaning God gives them a child.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور بفتح الباء وشد الدال. وقرأ عاصم بسكون الباء وتخفيف الدال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The replacement child is better in zakat, meaning religion and righteousness, and nearer in rahm, meaning mercy.
rows.anchor: أي دينا وصلاحا يقال: بدل وأبدل مثل مهل وأمهل ونزل وأنزل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reads rahma with a ḍamma; other readers use sukūn.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عباس «رحما» بالضم

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A line about a wronged young woman witnesses rahm with a ḍamma.
rows.anchor: وكيف بظلم جارية ومنها اللين والرحم

rows.speaker: رؤبة بن العجاج
rows.claim: A line by Ru'ba witnesses the sukūn reading of rahm.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول رؤبة بن العجاج: يا منزل الرحم على إدريسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahm is coordinated with zakat and means mercy; it may instead mean kinship, as Ibn Abbas's variant indicates.
rows.anchor: و«رحما» معطوف على «زكاة» أي رحمة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported with readings “more closely joined in kinship” and “more pure than him.”
rows.anchor: قرأها ابن عباس «وأوصل رحما» أي رحما، وقرأ أيضا «أزكى منه»

rows.speaker: ابن جبير وابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Jurayj say God replaced the boy with a girl; al-Kalbi says she married a prophet and bore a prophet through whom a nation was guided.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن جبير وابن جريج أنهما بدلا جارية قال الكلبي فتزوجها نبي من الأنبياء

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the replacement girl gave birth to twelve prophets.
rows.anchor: قتادة: ولدت اثني عشر نبيا

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj also says the mother was pregnant with a Muslim boy when the disbelieving boy was killed.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن جريج أيضا أن أم الغلام يوم قتل كانت حاملا بغلام مسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a girl was born who in turn bore a prophet; another report says she bore seventy prophets.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس: فولدت جارية ولدت نبيا

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد عن أبيه
rows.claim: Ja'far ibn Muhammad transmits from his father the report that the replacement daughter bore seventy prophets.
rows.anchor: جعفر بن محمد عن أبيه قال علماؤنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi's scholars call the seventy-prophet report far-fetched because such a number is known only among Israelites, and this woman was not among them.
rows.anchor: وهذا بعيد ولا تعرف كثرة الأنبياء إلا في بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage teaches that losing children can be borne more lightly when one submits to God's decree, whose outcome may be good.
rows.anchor: ويستفاد من هذه الآية تهوين المصائب بفقد الأولاد وإن كانوا قطعا من الأكباد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the parents rejoiced at birth and grieved at death, yet had the boy lived he would have destroyed them; what God decrees despite dislike is better for a believer.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: لقد فرح به أبواه حين ولد وحزنا عليه حين قتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boys were apparently minors because the verse calls them orphans, though orphan status may remain as a compassionate description after puberty; for humans it is loss of father, for animals of mother.
rows.anchor: هذان الغلامان صغيران بقرينة وصفهما باليتم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet's saying “no orphanhood after puberty” supports the inference that the boys were children.
rows.anchor: لا يتم بعد بلوغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word madina shows that qarya can also mean a city.
rows.anchor: أن القرية تسمى مدينة ومنه الحديث

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A hadith describes a qarya that consumes other settlements.
rows.anchor: أمرت بقرية تأكل القرى

rows.speaker: رجل
rows.claim: In the migration report, a man says he is from the people of Medina, meaning Mecca.
rows.anchor: فقال الرجل: من أهل المدينة

rows.speaker: عكرمة وقتادة
rows.claim: Ikrima and Qatada interpret the treasure as substantial material wealth, the apparent lexical meaning of kanz.
rows.anchor: فقال عكرمة وقتادة: كان مالا جسيما وهو الظاهر من اسم الكنز

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas instead says the treasure was knowledge written on buried pages.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: كان علما في صحف مدفونة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report describes a gold tablet inscribed with maxims about providence, provision, death, judgment, and worldly instability.
rows.anchor: كان لوحا من ذهب مكتوبا فيه بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: عثمان بن عفان
rows.claim: A similar tablet report is transmitted by Uthman from the Prophet, and versions come from Ikrima and Umar, freedman of Ghufra.
rows.anchor: وروي نحوه عن عكرمة وعمر مولى غفرة، ورواه عثمان بن عفان رضي الله عنه عن النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of “their father” is their immediate father.
rows.anchor: ظاهر اللفظ والسابق منه أنه والدهما دنية

rows.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
rows.claim: Ja'far ibn Muhammad identifies their father as their seventh ancestor; another view calls him the tenth ancestor, Kashih, according to Muqatil.
rows.anchor: هو الأب السابع قاله جعفر بن محمد. وقيل: العاشر

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash gives the boys' mother's name as Dunya.
rows.anchor: واسم أمهما دنيا ذكره النقاش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story indicates God protects a righteous person in himself and in distant descendants.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى يحفظ الصالح في نفسه وفي ولده وإن بعدوا عنه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A report says God preserves a righteous person through seven generations; Qurtubi connects this to the verse on God's guardianship of the righteous.
rows.anchor: وقد روي أن الله تعالى يحفظ الصالح في سبعة من ذريته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr's statement that he did not act on his own authority implies that he was a prophet.
rows.anchor: يقتضي أن الخضر نبي وقد تقدم الخلاف في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use the shortened reading tastaṭiʿ in keeping with the codex.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «تسطع» قال أبو حاتم: كذا نقرأ كما في خط المصحف

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima asks Ibn Abbas why Moses' companion is omitted; Ibn Abbas says the youth drank from the water of life and became immortal, then the sage sealed him in a boat and sent him into the sea until Resurrection because he drank what he was not allowed.
rows.anchor: فقال عكرمة لابن عباس: لم يسمع لفتى موسى بذكر وقد كان معه؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr ascribes the wall's erection to God because it concerns a distant unseen future; alternatively, he attributes wholly good work to God but the ship's defect to himself as good etiquette.
rows.anchor: إنما أسند الإرادة في الجدار إلى الله تعالى لأنها في أمر مستأنف في زمن طويل غيب من الغيوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attribution of the ship's defect to himself follows the etiquette of avoiding an unattractive attribution, as Abraham said that when he became ill God healed him.
rows.anchor: كما تأدب إبراهيم عليه السلام في قوله: وإذا مرضت فهو يشفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse “in Your hand is good” mentions good without mentioning evil, although all benefit and harm are under God's power.
rows.anchor: واقتصر عليه فلم ينسب الشر إليه، وإن كان بيده الخير والشر والضر والنفع

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The hadith in which God says “I was ill” is gracious indirect address teaching the value of visiting the sick, feeding the hungry, and giving drink to the thirsty.
rows.anchor: يا ابن آدم مرضت فلم تعدني واستطعمتك فلم تطعمني واستسقيتك فلم تسقني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may describe himself as he wills, while people should use only beautiful descriptions and noble actions authorized for him.
rows.anchor: ولله تعالى أن يطلق على نفسه ما يشاء، ولا نطلق نحن إلا ما أذن لنا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “we intended,” Khidr associates killing with himself and replacement with God; maturity means completeness of body and reason.
rows.anchor: وقال في الغلام: «فأردنا» فكأنه أضاف القتل إلى نفسه، والتبديل إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abu al-Abbas warns that esoteric antinomians claim ordinary law binds the masses but saints may dispense with scripture and follow inner inspiration, appealing to Khidr.
rows.anchor: ذهب قوم من زنادقة الباطنية إلى سلوك طريق تلزم منه هدم الأحكام الشرعية

rows.speaker: الزنادقة
rows.claim: The esoteric group cites “consult your heart even if the jurists advise you” and claims saints' pure hearts reveal rulings without general legal texts.
rows.anchor: استفت قلبك وإن أفتاك المفتون

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abu al-Abbas calls the antinomian claim heresy and unbelief deserving execution without a chance to recant, because it denies known religious law.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول زندقة وكفر يقتل قائله ولا يستتاب

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Religious rulings are known only through God's chosen messengers, whom God sends to teach law and commands.
rows.anchor: بأن أحكامه لا تعلم إلا بواسطة رسله السفراء بينه وبين خلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi invokes verses on God's selection of messengers, knowledge of where to place revelation, and humanity's need for prophetic warning.
rows.anchor: الله يصطفي من الملائكة رسلا ومن الناس إن الله سميع بصير

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Consensus says God's commands cannot be known except through messengers; claiming another route that makes them unnecessary is unbelief.
rows.anchor: وإجماع السلف والخلف على أن لا طريق لمعرفة أحكام الله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: A person who follows the heart as God's ruling without scripture or sunna effectively claims prophethood, resembling the Prophet's report of Holy Spirit inspiration.
rows.anchor: إن روح القدس نفث في روعي

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most people hold that Khidr died; another group says he remains alive after drinking from the spring of life and performs pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: ذهب الجمهور من الناس إلى أن الخضر مات

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya dismisses al-Naqqash's stories as unsupported and says an alive pilgrim would have appeared in Islam.
rows.anchor: وكلها لا تقوم على ساق

rows.speaker: البخاري
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari and hadith scholars including Ibn al-Arabi use the hundred-year report to argue that Khidr died.
rows.anchor: إلى هذا ذهب البخاري واختاره القاضي أبو بكر بن العربي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says the correct view is that Khidr is alive.
rows.anchor: والصحيح القول الثاني وهو أنه حي على ما نذكره

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Muslim's report says the Prophet prayed late-night prayer late in his life and said that at the head of a hundred years none alive on earth then would remain.
rows.anchor: صلى بنا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ذات ليلة صلاة العشاء في آخر حياته

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar says people misunderstood the statement as a full century; the Prophet meant the generation then alive would pass away.
rows.anchor: لا يبقى ممن هو اليوم على ظهر الأرض أحد

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jabir reports that a month before his death the Prophet said no living soul on earth would reach a hundred years; variants clarify those alive that day were meant.
rows.anchor: ورواه أيضا من حديث جابر بن عبد الله قال: سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول قبل أن يموت بشهر

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن صاحب السقاية
rows.claim: Abd al-Rahman interprets the report as shortening of lifespans; a parallel report is attributed to Abu Sa'id.
rows.anchor: وفسرها عبد الرحمن صاحب السقاية قال: نقص العمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi applies the hadith to humans alive when spoken, not angels, jinn, or non-rational animals; Ibn Umar understands it as that generation's end.
rows.anchor: وحاصل ما تضمنه هذا الحديث أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام أخبر قبل موته بشهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: General wording admits specification, as with Jesus and the Dajjal; Khidr is hidden from ordinary contact, and reports also say the Cave Companions and Moses' companion survive.
rows.anchor: لأن العموم وإن كان مؤكد الاستغراق فليس نصا فيه، بل هو قابل للتخصيص

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: Al-Tha'labi calls Khidr a long-lived prophet hidden from sight; a report says he is Persian and Elijah Israelite, meeting annually at pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن الخضر نبي معمر محجوب عن الأبصار

rows.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
rows.claim: Amr ibn Dinar says Khidr and Elijah remain alive as long as the Quran remains, and die when it is lifted.
rows.anchor: وعن عمرو بن دينار قال: إن الخضر وإلياس لا يزالان حيين في الأرض

rows.speaker: أبو محمد عبد المعطي اللخمي
rows.claim: Abu Muhammad al-Lakhmi recounts many encounters with Khidr by righteous people; together with other reports, they make his survival probable.
rows.anchor: حكايات كثيرة عن جماعة من الصالحين والصالحات بأنهم رأوا الخضر عليه السلام ولقوه

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq identifies as Khidr the exceptionally good man whom a Muslim hadith says will confront the Dajjal near Medina.
rows.anchor: وفي آخره قال أبو إسحاق: يعني أن هذا الرجل هو الخضر

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: A report says Ali met Khidr and learned a supplication to say after prayer, promising great reward, forgiveness, and mercy; a similar report is attributed to Umar.
rows.anchor: بسند يرفعه إلى علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه لقي الخضر وعلمه هذا الدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Elijah survived to the Prophet's time, Khidr could have too; they are said to meet yearly at the Kaaba and exchange words of reliance on God.
rows.anchor: وإذا جاز بقاء إلياس إلى عهد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم جاز بقاء الخضر

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ibn Abd al-Barr transmits Ali's story of an unseen caller comforting the Prophet's household after his death, whom the Companions took to be Khidr.
rows.anchor: هتف هاتف من ناحية البيت يسمعون صوته ولا يرون شخصه

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: The unseen caller's consolation says God replaces each loss and comforts every calamity; companions thought the caller was Khidr.
rows.anchor: إن في الله خلفا من كل هالك، وعوضا من كل تالف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the hundred-year report, “the earth” can mean familiar Arabia, not remote regions of Gog and Magog or far Indian islands.
rows.anchor: والألف واللام في قوله: «على الأرض» للعهد لا للجنس وهي أرض العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi admits his discussion has not answered the objection posed by the Dajjal report.
rows.anchor: ولا جواب عن الدجال

rows.speaker: ابن منبه
rows.claim: Al-Suhayli gives competing genealogies and legends of Khidr's birth from a king and Persian wife, including a foundling suckled by a sheep.
rows.anchor: فعن ابن منبه أنه قال: أيليا بن ملكان بن فالغ بن شالخ

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A legend says Khidr found the spring of life, remained alive until the Dajjal, and will be killed by him before God revives him.
rows.anchor: إلى أن وجد عين الحياة فشرب منها، فهو حي إلى أن يخرج الدجال

rows.speaker: البخاري وابن العربي
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari and Ibn al-Arabi say Khidr died before the hundred years elapsed; Qurtubi reiterates his contrary view that Khidr lives to the present.
rows.anchor: وقال البخاري وطائفة من أهل الحديث منهم شيخنا أبو بكر بن العربي رحمه الله تعالى: إنه مات

rows.speaker: الخضر
rows.claim: A farewell saying advises Moses to smile rather than laugh, avoid needless argument and travel, and grieve for his own sins rather than criticize sinners.
rows.anchor: قال له موسى: أوصني قال: كن بساما ولا تكن ضحاكا، ودع اللجاجة

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says Dhu al-Qarnayn received extraordinary means, traveled to the ends of the inhabited east and west, and gained authority over each people he reached.
rows.anchor: وكان من خبر ذي القرنين أنه أوتي ما لم يؤت غيره، فمدت له الأسباب

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: An account from Persian lore identifies him as Marzuban ibn Mardabah, an Egyptian of Greek descent from Yunan son of Japheth; Ibn Hisham instead calls him Alexander, founder of Alexandria.
rows.anchor: أن ذا القرنين كان رجلا من أهل مصر اسمه مرزبان بن مردبة اليوناني

rows.speaker: خالد بن معدان الكلاعي
rows.claim: Khalid ibn Ma'dan transmits a report that the Prophet called him a king who traversed earth by pathways; Ibn Ishaq doubts whether it is genuinely Prophetic.
rows.anchor: عن خالد بن معدان الكلاعي وكان خالد رجلا قد أدرك الناس أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم سئل

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar rebuked someone addressed as Dhu al-Qarnayn, asking whether people were not satisfied with prophetic names before taking angel names.
rows.anchor: وسمع عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله تعالى عنه رجلا يقول: يا ذا القرنين

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali is also reported to have rebuked the title by analogy with taking names of prophets and angels.
rows.anchor: روي عن علي بن أبي طالب رضي الله تعالى عنه مثل قول عمر

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali calls him a righteous servant and king, supported by God; another view makes him a prophet through whose hands God opened the earth.
rows.anchor: وعنه أنه عبد ملك بكسر اللام صالح نصح الله فأيده

rows.speaker: الدارقطني
rows.claim: Al-Daraqutni says angel Rabaqil visited Dhu al-Qarnayn and is the angel who will fold and diminish the earth on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: أن ملكا يقال له رباقيل كان ينزل على ذي القرنين

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhayli compares Rabaqil's assignment to Dhu al-Qarnayn with Malik's assignment to Khalid ibn Sinan, who subdued the fire.
rows.anchor: وهذا مشاكل بتوكيله بذي القرنين الذي قطع الأرض مشارقها ومغاربها

rows.speaker: ابن أبي خيثمة
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Khaythama says Khalid ibn Sinan extinguished the Fire of Hadathan, which emerged from a cave and consumed people; Malik, keeper of Hell, was assigned to him.
rows.anchor: وكان من أعلام نبوته أن نارا يقال لها نار الحدثان، كانت تخرج على الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name of Dhu al-Qarnayn and its reason are matters of extensive disagreement; one identification is Alexander the Macedonian king.
rows.anchor: واختلف في اسم ذي القرنين وفي السبب الذي سمي به بذلك اختلافا كثيرا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Names proposed for Dhu al-Qarnayn include Hermes and Hirdis; Ibn Hisham names him al-Sa'b ibn Dhi Yazan of Himyar, while Wahb calls him Roman.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اسمه هرمس. ويقال: اسمه هرديس

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Al-Tabari transmits a hadith calling him a Roman youth, which Ibn Atiyya judges to have a weak chain.
rows.anchor: وذكر الطبري حديثا عن النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام: أن ذا القرنين شاب من الروم

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhayli thinks the reports describe two rulers: one in Abraham's time, who judged the well dispute, and another near Jesus' time.
rows.anchor: والظاهر من علم الأخبار أنهما اثنان: أحدهما: كان على عهد إبراهيم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One identification is Afridun, who killed the tyrant king Biyurasb around Abraham's time.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه أفريدون الذي قتل بيوراسب بن أرونداسب الملك الطاغي

rows.speaker: الثعلبي وغيره
rows.claim: One explanation for the title is that he had two braids or locks of hair; a poem uses qurun for those locks.
rows.anchor: فقيل: إنه كان ذا ضفيرتين من شعر فسمي بهما

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another says he dreamed of grasping the sun's two horns and was told this meant he would rule what the sun reaches.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه رأى في أول ملكه كأنه قابض على قرني الشمس

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that reaching both west and east meant he possessed the world's two horns.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنما سمي بذلك لأنه بلغ المغرب والمشرق فكأنه حاز قرني الدنيا

rows.speaker: طائفة
rows.claim: A group says he saw the sun's horns at sunrise and was named for them or the devil's horns there.
rows.anchor: وقالت طائفة: إنه لما بلغ مطلع الشمس كشف بالرؤية قرونها

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says he wore two horns beneath his turban.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب بن منبه: كان له قرنان تحت عمامته

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali says he was neither prophet nor king but a righteous servant who called his people to God; they split his head twice, giving him the title.
rows.anchor: لا ذا ولا ذا، كان عبدا صالحا دعا قومه إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: His era is variously placed after Moses, after Jesus, or during Abraham and Ishmael's time; Khidr is said to have carried his chief banner.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا أيضا في وقت زمانه، فقال قوم: كان بعد موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says God empowered him and reports four world rulers: Solomon and Alexander, and Nimrod and Nebuchadnezzar.
rows.anchor: فإن الله تعالى مكنه وملكه ودانت له الملوك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Mahdi is expected as a fifth world ruler from this community, based on the verse that God will make the religion prevail.
rows.anchor: وسيملكها من هذه الأمة خامس لقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other explanations say he was noble on both sides, outlived two generations, fought with both arms and stirrups, knew outward and hidden matters, entered darkness and light, or ruled Persia and Rome.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل: إنما سمي ذا القرنين لأنه كان كريم الطرفين من أهل بيت شريف

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali says God subjected clouds, opened paths, spread light, and made night and day alike for him.
rows.anchor: قال علي رضي الله عنه: سخر له السحاب، ومدت له الأسباب، وبسط له في النور

rows.speaker: عقبة بن عامر
rows.claim: A report from Uqba says the Prophet told the People of the Book Dhu al-Qarnayn was a Roman youth, received kingship, built Alexandria, and was shown the earth by an angel before being told to travel and teach.
rows.anchor: سألوه عن ذي القرنين فقال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the means as knowledge to reach whatever he wanted.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: من كل شيء علما يتسبب به إلى ما يريد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says they were means to reach wherever he wished.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: بلاغا إلى حيث أراد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other explanations say the means were what creatures need or royal instruments for conquering cities and enemies.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من كل شيء يحتاج إليه الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sabab literally means rope and was extended metaphorically to anything by which one reaches an end.
rows.anchor: وأصل السبب الحبل فاستعير لكل ما يتوصل به إلى شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Amir, Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read fa-atbaʿa with separated hamza; Medinans and Abu Amr read fa-ttabaʿa with connected hamza, meaning he followed a route.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي «فأتبع سببا» مقطوعة الألف

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash treats tabaʿa and atbaʿa as synonyms, like radifa and ardafa, and cites a shooting star.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش: تبعته وأتبعته بمعنى مثل ردفته وأردفته

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd prefers the Kufan reading because it denotes travel and cites al-Asma'i's distinction between walking without catching and pursuing until one catches up.
rows.anchor: واختار أبو عبيد قراءة أهل الكوفة قال: لأنها من السير

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas says the distinction between following and catching up should not be accepted without evidence.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: وهذا من التفريق وإن كان الأصمعي قد حكاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The correct view is that tabaʿa, ittabaʿa, and atbaʿa are dialects meaning to proceed, whether or not catching up occurs.
rows.anchor: والحق في هذا أن تبع واتبع وأتبع لغات بمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Pharaoh example does not show the pursuers caught up; the three forms mean proceeding.
rows.anchor: ليس في الحديث أنهم لحقوهم، وإنما الحديث: لما خرج موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Asim, Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read hāmiyah, “hot”; other readers say ḥami'ah, “muddy,” with black mud.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عاصم وعامر وحمزة والكسائي «حامية» أي حارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb forms distinguish removing mud from a well and a well becoming muddy; hāmiyah may derive from ham'a with a lightened hamza, allowing both senses.
rows.anchor: تقول: حمأت البئر حمأ بالتسكين إذا نزعت حمأتها

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: Abdullah ibn Amr reports that the Prophet called the setting sun God's heated fire, held back from burning the earth by God's command.
rows.anchor: نار الله الحامية لولا ما يزعها من أمر الله لأحرقت ما على الأرض

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Ubayy taught him the reading ʿayn ḥamiʾah as the Prophet taught Ubayy.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: أقرأنيها أبي كما أقرأه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم «في عين حمئة»

rows.speaker: كعب
rows.claim: When Muawiya favored hāmiyah, Abdullah ibn Amr asked Ka'b to arbitrate by the Torah; Ka'b said it sets in a black spring, agreeing with Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: فقال عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص: فأنا مع أمير المؤمنين فجعلوا كعبا بينهم حكما

rows.speaker: تبع اليماني
rows.claim: A poem by Tubba al-Yamani describes the sun disappearing in a spring with mud and black mire; its words are glossed as mud, mire, and black.
rows.anchor: فرأى مغيب الشمس عند غروبها في عين ذي خلب وثأط حرمد

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal says the sun does not physically reach the earth because it is vastly larger and moves with the celestial sphere; Dhu al-Qarnayn reached the western edge of habitation, where it only looked as if the sun sank into a muddy spring.
rows.anchor: ليس المراد أنه انتهى إلى الشمس مغربا ومشرقا حتى وصل إلى جرمها ومسها

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Saying the sun rose upon a people means they were the first people it reached, not that it physically touched them.
rows.anchor: بل أراد أنهم أول من تطلع عليهم

rows.speaker: القتبي
rows.claim: Al-Qutbi allows that the spring could be part of the sea and the sun set beyond, with, or near it, with one preposition standing for another.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون هذه العين من البحر

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: The people near the western spring are identified as inhabitants of Jabras, called Jirjisa in Syriac and descended from the remnant of Thamud who believed in Salih.
rows.anchor: وهم أهل جابرس، ويقال لها بالسريانية: جرجيسا

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb's account describes nations across earth: longitudinal Nasik and Mansik, lateral Hawil and Tawil, and central peoples including jinn, humans, and Gog and Magog.
rows.anchor: وهم أمم جميع الأرض، وهم أصناف: أمتان بينهما طول الأرض كله، وأمتان بينهما عرض الأرض كله

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: God promised him understanding of every language, an unshakable heart, and light and darkness as armies, one guiding and the other guarding him.
rows.anchor: سأظفرك بما حملتك أشرح لك صدرك فتسمع كل شيء

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: He subdued western Nasik with darkness and brought them to faith with light, then formed them into an army and traveled with darkness behind and light ahead.
rows.anchor: فكاثرهم بالظلمة فضرب حولهم ثلاث عساكر من جند الظلمة

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb says he similarly subdued eastern Hawil and other nations before turning to central peoples.
rows.anchor: فانتهى إلى هاويل وفعل بهم كفعله بناسك فآمنوا

rows.speaker: أمة صالحة من الإنس
rows.claim: A righteous human community warns that countless animal-like Gog and Magog eat animals and creatures, multiply rapidly, and may drive humans from earth; they offer tribute for a barrier.
rows.anchor: إن بين هذين الجبلين خلقا من خلق الله تعالى كثيرا ليس لهم عدد

rows.speaker: القشيري أبو نصر
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri says God's address to Dhu al-Qarnayn would be revelation if he was a prophet and inspiration if not.
rows.anchor: إن كان نبيا فهو وحي، وإن لم يكن نبيا فهو إلهام من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: إبراهيم بن السري
rows.claim: Ibrahim ibn al-Sarri compares the choice to punish or act kindly with the Prophet's choice whether to judge the People of the Book or turn away.
rows.anchor: خيره بين هذين كما خير محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj takes the passage as God giving Dhu al-Qarnayn a choice between two judgments.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحق الزجاج: المعنى أن الله تعالى خيره بين هذين الحكمين

rows.speaker: علي بن سليمان
rows.claim: Ali ibn Sulayman objects that Dhu al-Qarnayn is not proven a prophet, making divine address and his punishment language problematic.
rows.anchor: ورد علي بن سليمان عليه قوله لأنه لم يصح أن ذا القرنين نبي

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas proposes that God told Muhammad that others said these words to Dhu al-Qarnayn.
rows.anchor: التقدير قلنا يا محمد قالوا يا ذا القرنين

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر النحاس
rows.claim: Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas says the objection fails: God could speak through a contemporary prophet or address him as in the prisoner-release verse; he offered execution for persistent unbelief and kindness for repentance.
rows.anchor: هذا الذي قاله أبو الحسن لا يلزم منه شيء

rows.speaker: أحمد بن يحيى
rows.claim: Ahmad ibn Yahya says “either you punish” is accusative, though nominative also works if “it is” is elided, as in the cited poem.
rows.anchor: ولو رفعت كان صوابا بمعنى فإما هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Medinan readers, Abu Amr, and Asim read jazāʾ al-ḥusnā in the nominative as a construct phrase; al-husna can mean Paradise, good deeds, or reward Dhu al-Qarnayn grants.
rows.anchor: قراءة أهل المدينة وأبي عمرو وعاصم «فله جزاء الحسنى» بالرفع على الابتداء أو بالاستقرار

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra takes al-husna as Paradise and compares the phrase to “certainty of certainty” and “the abode of the afterlife.”
rows.anchor: أي له جزاء الحسنى عند الله تعالى في الآخرة وهي الجنة

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Ishaq reads jazāʾ al-ḥusnā in nominative with tanwin; Qurtubi calls it better than deleting tanwin before the construct.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا قراءة ابن أبي إسحاق «فله جزاء الحسنى» إلا أنك لم تحذف التنوين

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Other Kufans read jazāʾ al-ḥusnā in the accusative with tanwin, taking jazāʾ as specification.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: «جزاء» منصوب على التمييز

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj analyzes the accusative as a verbal noun functioning adverbially, meaning he is rewarded with it as reward.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: هو مصدر في موضع الحال أي مجزيا بها جزاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومسروق
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Masruq read jazāʾ in the accusative without tanwin.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس ومسروق «فله جزاء الحسنى» منصوبا غير منون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Atbaʿa here means he took a route and passed through stages.
rows.anchor: تقدم معناه أن أتبع واتبع بمعنى، أي سلك طريقا ومنازل

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن محيصن
rows.claim: Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin read maṭliʿ with both mīm and lām opened; it can mean sunrise or its place.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد وابن محيصن بفتح الميم واللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reached a place with no people between it and sunrise; the sun rose far beyond them, so the verse means it rose on them first.
rows.anchor: المعنى أنه انتهى إلى موضع قوم لم يكن بينهم وبين مطلع الشمس أحد من الناس

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه ومقاتل
rows.claim: Wahb and Muqatil call the eastern people Mansik, paired with western Nasik.
rows.anchor: وأنها أمة يقال لها منسك وهي مقابلة ناسك وقاله مقاتل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada calls them the Zanj.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: يقال لهما الزنج

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies Taris, Hawil, and Mansik and describes them as barefoot, naked, and blind to truth, with animal-like sexual behavior.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: هم تارس وهاويل ومنسك حفاة عراة عماة عن الحق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view identifies people of Jablaq as descendants of believers of Aad who followed Hud; their western counterparts lived in Jabras.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هم أهل جابلق، وهم من نسل مؤمني عاد الذين آمنوا بهود

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhayli says Jabras and Jablaq each had ten thousand gates, a parasang apart; other peoples behind Jablaq neighbored Gog and Magog.
rows.anchor: ولكل واحدة من المدينتين عشرة آلاف باب، بين كل بابين فرسخ

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhayli says Jabras and Jablaq believed in the Prophet on the Night Journey while other nations refused, citing a long report through Muqatil ibn Hayyan, Ikrima, and Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: وأهل جابرس وجابلق آمنوا بالنبي عليه الصلاة والسلام مر بهم ليلة الإسراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They had no curtain or shelter shielding them from the rising sun.
rows.anchor: أي حجابا يستترون منها عند طلوعها

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says they lived in burrows and returned to work and cultivation after midday, rather than hiding in caves, mountains, or houses.
rows.anchor: حتى إذا زالت الشمس عنهم رجعوا إلى معايشهم

rows.speaker: أمية
rows.claim: Umayya recounts travelers beyond China who saw people rest their ears beneath them; after a strange sound and fainting, they saw sunrise on water like oil, then people sheltered underground and fished in the sun.
rows.anchor: فوجدت أحدهم يفترش أذنه ويلتحف بالأخرى

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says an army was warned not to stay until sunrise and fled on seeing bones of an army that died there.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: جاءهم جيش مرة، فقال لهم أهلها: لا تطلع الشمس وأنتم بها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says the land lacked mountains, trees, and buildings; its people entered water at sunrise and came out to graze like animals.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: كانت أرضهم لا جبل فيها ولا شجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi concludes there was no city there; some may have sheltered in the river and others in burrows, reconciling Hasan and Qatada.
rows.anchor: قلت: وهذه الأقوال تدل على أن لا مدينة هناك
